extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in enumerative combinatorics / advanced undergraduate or graduate combinatorics course
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, bijections, enumerative formulas, and combinatorial constructions for permutation statistics (inversions, descents, major index, Eulerian numbers, pattern-avoidance, tree and matrix representations) used to count and relate permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proof techniques for equality of polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic ways of giving a combinatorial proof that two polynomials are equal: (i) showing that their coefficients are equal, and (ii) showing that they agree for sufficiently many values of their variable(s). If two polynomials in a single variable t (over the complex numbers, say) agree for all t in P (sufficiently many values), then they agree as polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply technique (ii) by evaluating at sufficiently many t ∈ P; the text uses this to establish Proposition 1.3.7 by counting combinatorial objects for each t. Example: establish (1.28) for all t ∈ P so the polynomials must be identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm mapping integer sequences to permutation+cycle-labeling (bijection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence (a1,...,an) with 0 ≤ ai ≤ t + i − 1, define a permutation w and a function f:C(w)→{1,...,t} by iteratively inserting elements n,n−1,...,1 into disjoint-cycle notation using two rules depending on ai (whether ai ≤ t+i−1 or equals t+k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: start with n as cycle C1 and set f(C1)=an+1; when inserting next element either start a new cycle to the left and set its f-value, or insert into an existing cycle so it's not the leftmost and positioned to the right of k+1 previously inserted numbers. The procedure gives a bijection (illustrated by the worked example n=9,t=4,(a1,...,a9)=(4,8,5,0,7,5,2,4,1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration of sequences with exactly k zeros (Proposition 1.3.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let n,k ≥ 0. The number of integer sequences (a1,...,an) with 0 ≤ ai ≤ i−1 and exactly k values of ai equal 0 is c(n,k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields by Proposition 1.3.1 the enumeration of permutations by left-to-right maxima: the number of w ∈ Sn with k left-to-right maxima is c(n,k) (Corollary 1.3.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion table and bijection I: Sn → Tn (Proposition 1.3.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define I(w) = (a1,...,an) where ai is the number of entries j to the left of i in the word representation of w satisfying j > i (equivalently, ai counts j to left of i with wj > wi). The map I is a bijection between Sn and Tn = { (a1,...,an): 0 ≤ ai ≤ n − i }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction algorithm: build w from its inversion table by inserting elements; example sequences and resulting permutations are shown. The inversion table provides an alternative canonical encoding of a permutation; the code(w)=I(w^{-1}) is similarly defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: q-analogue notion and desirable property
rubrics_metrics.description: A q-analogue of a mathematical object is an object depending on q that 'reduces to' the original object when q=1. More is usually required for a 'satisfactory' q-analogue: the original should concern finite sets while the q-analogue can be interpreted in terms of subspaces of finite-dimensional vector spaces over Fq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (n)! = (1+q)(1+q+q^2)⋯(1+q+⋯+q^{n−1}) is regarded as a satisfactory q-analogue of n! because when q is a prime power (n)! counts flags V0⊂V1⊂...⊂Vn=F_q^n with dim Vi = i. No precise formal definition is given, but interpretability over finite fields is a desirable criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descent and ascent sets, α(S) and β(S) counts
rubrics_metrics.description: For w=w1...wn ∈ Sn, i is a descent if wi > wi+1 and an ascent if wi < wi+1 (with indices 1..n−1). The descent set D(w) = { i : wi > wi+1 } ⊆ [n−1]. Define α(S) = #{w ∈ Sn : D(w) ⊆ S} and β(S) = #{w ∈ Sn : D(w)=S}. Then α(S) = ∑_{T⊆S} β(T) and β(S)=∑_{T⊆S} (−1)^{|S−T|} α(T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 1.4.1 gives a product formula for α(S) when S={s1<...<sk} as α(S)=C(n,s1) C(n−s1, s2−s1) ... C(n−sk, n−sk). Examples and inversion relations provided; see formulas (1.31)–(1.35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating and reverse alternating permutations and Euler numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: A permutation w is alternating (down-up) if w1>w2<w3>... (i.e., D(w) = {1,3,5,...}∩[n−1]); reverse alternating (up-down) if w1<w2>w3<.... The number of alternating permutations in Sn is denoted En and called an Euler number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: w is alternating iff n+1 − w is reverse alternating, so En counts both types appropriately. Small examples for S4 are given. Euler numbers appear in later sections (e.g., Section 1.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eulerian polynomials and Eulerian numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Ad(x)=∑_{w∈Sd} x^{1+des(w)} = ∑_{k} A(d,k) x^k where A(d,k) is the number of permutations in Sd with exactly k−1 descents (Eulerian number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of small Ad(x) polynomials is provided (A0..A8). Proposition 1.4.4 gives the ordinary generating function ∑_{m≥0} m^d x^m = Ad(x)/(1−x)^{d+1} (equation 1.37). Differentiation yields recursive identity Ad+1(x)=x(1−x)A'_d(x)+(d+1)x A_d(x) leading to recurrence A(d+1,k)=k A(d,k) + (d−k+2) A(d,k−1) (equation 1.39) with combinatorial insertion interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major index maj(w) and equidistribution with inv(w)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define maj(w)=∑_{i∈D(w)} i (the sum of descent positions). The statistics inv (number of inversions) and maj are equidistributed on Sn: ∑_{w∈Sn} q^{inv(w)} = ∑_{w∈Sn} q^{maj(w)} = (n)! (q-factorial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 1.4.6 proves qmaj(w) = (n)! by constructing an explicit bijection ϕ:Sn→Sn with maj(w)=inv(ϕ(w)). The equality is also shown via generating functions (equation 1.42).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijection ϕ (γ-compartment algorithm) transforming maj to inv
rubrics_metrics.description: Define words γ1,...,γn where γ1=w1 and recursively obtain γ_{k+1} from γ_k by splitting γ_k into compartments relative to wk+1 (split after letters greater or smaller than wk+1), cyclically shift each compartment one unit to the right, and append wk+1. The map ϕ(w)=γn is a bijection with maj(w)=inv(ϕ(w)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: w=683941725 leads through γ-sequence to ϕ(w)=364891725 and verifies maj(w)=inv(ϕ(w))=18. The bijection is invertible via reverse compartment splits and left cyclic shifts; details and inductive proof provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse descent set ID(w) and reading-sequence interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: ID(w)=D(w^{-1}); equivalently, read the numbers 1,2,...,n in w from left-to-right in their natural order, cycling back when necessary; the cumulative sizes (excluding the last) of these reading sequences form the reading set which equals ID(w).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for w=683941725 the reading sequences and cumulative counts are given yielding ID(w)={2,5,7}. ID(w) extends to arbitrary sequences of distinct integers by identifying with the permutation of the set of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: ϕ preserves inverse descent set (Theorem 1.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bijection ϕ defined above preserves the inverse descent set: for all w ∈ Sn, ID(w) = ID(ϕ(w)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on k comparing ID(γk) and ID(ηk) (where ηk = w1...wk). This property is used to deduce symmetric joint distributions (see Corollary 1.4.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric joint distribution criterion for two statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Two statistics f,g on a finite set S have a symmetric joint distribution if for all j,k, #{x∈S: f(x)=j, g(x)=k} = #{x∈S: f(x)=k, g(x)=j}; equivalently ∑_{x∈S} q^{f(x)} t^{g(x)} is symmetric in (q,t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bijection ψ:S→S with f(x)=g(ψ(x)) and g(x)=f(ψ(x)) proves symmetry. Using ϕ and its properties, (inv,maj), (inv,imaj) and (maj,imaj) are shown to have symmetric joint distributions (Corollary 1.4.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: w-compatible functions and unique permutation reconstruction (Definition & Lemma 1.4.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For w∈Sn, a function f:[n]→N is w-compatible if f(w1)≥f(w2)≥...≥f(wn) and f(wi)>f(wi+1) whenever i∈D(w). Given f:[n]→N there is a unique permutation w ∈ Sn for which f is w-compatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: partition [n] into ordered blocks where f is constant and then within each block arrange elements in increasing order; concatenating blocks yields the permutation w. This establishes a bijection between ordered partitions (set compositions) induced by f and the unique w.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration/formulae for Am(w) and generating relations (Lemma 1.4.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For w ∈ Sd and m≥0, Am(w) = #{f:[d]→[m] that are w-compatible} equals binomial(m+d−des(w), d). For generating series: ∑_{m≥0} |Am(w)| x^m = x^{1+des(w)}/(1−x)^{d+1} and ∑_{f∈Am(w)} q^{|f|} = q^{maj(w)} / (1−q)(1−q^2)...(1−q^d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs convert partially strictly decreasing sequences to weakly decreasing ones via index shifts; example w=4632715 illustrates the bijection g(j)=f(j)−h_j (h_j=number of descents to right) and summation gives the stated formulas (equations 1.45–1.47). These relations are used to prove Propositions 1.4.4 and 1.4.6 conceptually (by counting functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation matrix Pw and 321-avoiding permutations ↔ lattice paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Pw is the n×n (0,1)-matrix with (Pw)_{i,j}=1 iff w(i)=j. Replace 1's by X's and draw a lattice path Lw from upper-left to lower-right with steps east or south whose outside corners occur at top/right of squares on or above main diagonal containing X's. Permutations with no decreasing subsequence of length three (321-avoiding) correspond bijectively to lattice paths that do not pass below the main diagonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This converts permutation enumeration to lattice-path counting; number of such permutations f(n)=Catalan number Cn = (1/(n+1)) (2n choose n) (equation 1.52). Figures illustrate Pw and resulting paths; the bijection is reversible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram Dw of a permutation and relation to inversion table/code
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent w by an n×n array of dots at coordinates (i,j) for 1≤i,j≤n; if w(i)=j draw horizontal line to right and vertical line down from (i,j); the set of dots not covered by lines is the diagram Dw. If aj is number of dots of Dw in column j then I(w)=(a1,...,an) (inversion table); if ci is number in row i then code(w)=(c1,...,cn) (code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Dw to characterize pattern-avoidance: w is 132-avoiding iff Dw is a Ferrers diagram of a partition λ with λ1≥λ2≥... and λi ≤ n−i; then #Dw = inv(w) and enumeration of 132-avoiding permutations refines to partitions λ with bounds, counted by Catalan numbers as well. Figures and examples illustrate Dw and its relation to I(w).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tree representation T(w) (increasing binary tree) and correspondence to permutation features
rubrics_metrics.description: For w a word on distinct letters, define binary tree T(w): let i be the least element of w, factor w = u i v, make i the root, recursively set T(u) as left subtree and T(v) as right subtree. For w∈Sn this gives a bijection between Sn and increasing binary trees on n labelled vertices (labels increase along any root-to-leaf path).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading labels of T(w) in symmetric (inorder) order recovers w. Vertex properties correspond to permutation local patterns: element i is a double rise iff vertex i has only a right successor, double fall iff only left successor, valley iff both successors, peak iff none. Enumerative consequences (Proposition 1.5.3): (a) number of increasing binary trees with n vertices is n!; (b) number with exactly k vertices having left successors equals Eulerian number A(n,k+1); (c) number of complete increasing binary trees with 2n+1 vertices equals E_{2n+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unordered increasing tree T'(w) and structural correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an unordered tree T'(w) with vertices 0,1,...,n by making vertex i the child of the rightmost element j of w that precedes i and is less than i; if none exists attach i to root 0. This yields a bijection between Sn and increasing (unordered) trees on n+1 labelled vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: successors of root 0 are the left-to-right minima of w; endpoints of T'(w) correspond to elements wi that are right-to-left minima or lie at the end. Enumerative consequences (Proposition 1.5.5): (a) number of unordered increasing trees on n+1 vertices is n!; (b) number with root having k successors is signless Stirling number c(n,k); (c) number with k endpoints is Eulerian number A(n,k).
